articles.title: This Is the Right Time to Eat Dinner—And Chances Are, You’re *Way* Off. Here’s Why That’s a Big Problem
articles.content:
晚餐吃几点最好？早餐还是晚餐？在忙碌的工作、照顾孩子和其他生活事务中，你可能会随时抽空进餐，无论是什么时间。但或许你需要重新考虑这一点。

一项最新的YouGov民调显示，71%的受访者通常在晚上6点或更晚用晚餐。多年来，5点用餐一直被视为早餐特惠、老年折扣和餐厅人烟稀少的代名词，几乎可以独享整个餐厅。这通常是你取笑父母和祖父母的用餐时间，而非你自己会选择的。

但现在滚动浏览TikTok，你会发现年轻专业人士自豪地关掉工作，在阳光还没落山时就开始用餐，并在#EarlyDinner标签下分享。最近OpenTable的数据支持了你的信息流所展示的内容：53%的Z世代和51%的千禧一代表示他们特别青睐更早的预订，在纽约，5点的预订量上升了20%。一份Chase Travel报告甚至宣称“5:30 p.m.是新的8 p.m.”。

那么谁是对的？是退休社区在高尔夫比赛后早早用餐（以及Z世代拍摄5点预订）？还是坚持传统晚餐时间的大多数美国人？我们请来了专家来解决这个争论。接下来，五位医学专家，包括睡眠健康、神经科学和心理学领域的专家，将告诉我们晚餐的正确时间以及为什么它如此重要。

继续阅读，了解你应该准时用餐的具体时间。

《读者文摘》的Read Up通讯提供更多生活辩论、清洁、幽默、旅行、科技和趣味事实。

是的。我们采访的专家不断强调一个概念：你的身体运行在一个大约24小时的内部时钟上——你的昼夜节律——它不仅影响你感到清醒或困倦的时间，还影响你如何应对食物。

“褪黑素的分泌，即信号身体准备睡眠的激素，会被光和进食抑制。”莎拉·鲍斯（Sarah Boss）医生解释道，她是精神科医生和康复诊所The Balance的临床主任。换句话说，晚餐与睡眠时间的同步性确实很重要。

这取决于你的睡眠时间，但研究显示，方向非常明确：更早，并且在入睡前很久就结束。是的，根据科学研究，Z世代和你的祖母在6点前用餐竟然是一个真正的健康升级。

“晚餐会使胰岛素水平升高并延迟褪黑素分泌。”鲍斯医生说。吃得太晚会强迫你的身体同时做两件事——消化食物和管理血糖，而此时它正准备睡眠。

这比单一的时间点更个人化，但根据你的生活和睡眠时间，正确的时间安排非常重要。以下是原因。

这是最重要的一点。 “最一致的发现是，临近睡眠的一到两小时内进食大餐，更可能影响睡眠连续性。”阿维内什·巴尔（Avinesh Bhar）医生说，他是睡眠医生和Sliiip创始人。

如果你躺下时肚子里还有食物，你的消化系统正在加班工作，而你的身体想要关闭。 “消化会提高血糖、胰岛素、代谢活动和体温，而此时身体应该降温并准备睡眠。”迈克尔·布雷斯（Michael Breus）博士说，他是临床心理学家和睡眠专家，被称为“睡眠博士”。

背后还有一个激素交接过程。 “晚上，我们的皮质醇水平想要下降，以便大脑可以促进褪黑素的释放。”艾丽森·布拉格（Allison Brager）博士说，她是神经科学家和美国军队领先的睡眠专家。当你不忙于消化时，她解释说，白天的这些过程可以关闭，这样睡眠系统就可以启动。

你的身体在晚上处理糖的能力较差。胰岛素敏感性在早上达到峰值，在晚上下降，因此同样的食物在夜晚会比中午更容易使血糖升高。

证据非常显著：约翰斯·霍普金斯大学的研究人员发现，晚10点用餐后的餐后血糖比晚6点用餐时的相同餐食高出约18%。约翰斯·霍普金斯大学的同一团队进行了后续研究，发现熬夜并不能扭转这一效果，将责任归咎于昼夜节律错配，而不仅仅是睡前进食。

换句话说，就血糖而言，实际的时间点很重要——不仅仅是你睡前吃饭的时间。 “在褪黑素水平升高时进食会导致昼夜节律与代谢错配，并与较差的葡萄糖耐受性相关——特别是如果晚餐在习惯性入睡前两小时内。”巴尔医生说。

早餐并非减肥的魔法按钮——你的总摄入量仍然是最重要的。但时间安排似乎能起到关键作用。

伯明翰大学的研究人员发现，那些早餐的人比那些进食时间跨度更长的人平均减去了近14磅。2026年发表在《英国医学杂志》上的一篇对41项随机试验和超过2000名参与者的综述也发现，早餐比晚餐更有利于减肥和空腹胰岛素水平。

“在总日摄入量相同的情况下，早餐会比晚餐摄入相同数量的热量导致脂肪增加更少。”雅各布·泰特尔鲍姆（Jacob Teitelbaum）医生说，他是《从疲劳到精彩》的作者。 “早餐还能抑制你的食欲激素，这样你就不会在晚上过度进食。”

额外的好处？早餐也可以作为间歇性断食——无需刻意控制。 “现在有一种趋势是支持间歇性断食，即在12到14小时的时间窗口内进食。”布拉格医生说。 “早餐支持这一点，而无需刻意去做。”在晚上早些吃完晚餐，睡7到8个小时，就像她说的，“那里就有你的12小时断食时间窗。”

重力比你想象的做了更多的工作。 “躺下时，重力不再帮助保持胃内容物在膈肌下方。”巴尔医生说。 “睡眠也会减少吞咽和食管清除，因此酸性或非酸性返流更容易引起不适，导致微觉醒。”

大阪市立大学的一项研究发现，晚餐与睡眠之间的间隔小于三小时的人患返流病的几率比晚餐与睡眠间隔四小时或更长的人高出近7.5倍。

“我们的身体被设计为在中午午餐时摄入大部分热量。”泰特尔鲍姆医生说。 “随着我们从农村工业化并转向城市，这种情况发生了变化。午餐后小睡一觉对工厂老板来说不方便。”

如果你违背这种古老的节奏，你就要为它付出代价。实际上，布拉格医生指出，“轮班工作与肥胖症、糖尿病和溃疡高度相关，很大一部分原因是进食时间与我们未被编程的进食时间不同。”她直截了当地说，“我们的生物学从未被编程，也永远不会被编程为在夜晚进食。”

这不仅仅是轮班工作者的问题。巴塞罗那全球健康研究所的研究人员发现，晚餐时间晚于9点，而非8点之前，与心血管疾病的风险增加13%相关。

可能，但如果安排得当，早餐实际上可以缓解夜间饥饿，因为更稳定的血糖意味着更少的饥饿感。通常需要一个调整期。 “夜间饥饿在调整为早餐后通常需要两周的调整期，在此期间，身体的饥饿素模式——饥饿激素——会重新校准。”鲍斯医生说。

反直觉的是，晚餐可能会使你更饥饿。 “差劲的或碎片化的睡眠也会增加饥饿素和减少饱腹素，这是一种信号饱腹感的激素。”布雷斯医生说。 “晚餐有时会使你第二天早晨更饥饿——而不是更不饥饿。”在哈佛大学的一项研究中，推迟约4小时进食增加了饥饿感，并提高了饥饿素与饱腹素的比例。

如果你确实需要睡前进食，请谨慎选择。你应该选择低糖、高蛋白的食物，比如核桃或杏仁，布拉格医生说——而不是一碗冰淇淋。布雷斯医生和巴尔医生也喜欢这个公式：少量零食，约150到200卡路里，包括蛋白质和缓释碳水化合物，如希腊酸奶加几颗浆果、香蕉加一点坚果酱或一小碗燕麦片。布雷斯医生说，目标是“缓解真正的饥饿感，而不要求你的身体在睡眠时消化另一顿饭。”

把晚餐提前效果最好，当你的其他时间也随之调整。几个专家支持的调整：

令人放心的是，我们采访的所有专家都同意——关键在于间隔，而不是时间。

“固定餐食与你的睡眠时间。”巴尔医生说。 “在睡前两到四个小时完成一顿正常的晚餐是一个合理的起点。”布拉格医生将最佳时间定为睡前两到三小时，并简单地说，“越早越好。”鲍斯医生以一种不增加压力的方式表述：“对于一个午夜入睡的人来说，9点用餐在生理上相当于6点用餐对于9点入睡的人来说。”

如果你的晚餐确实无法在8点或9点之前进行，并且你不能熬夜来弥补，怎么办？ “把晚餐吃得更少。”布雷斯医生说。 “将更多的热量转移到早餐和午餐，然后选择以瘦蛋白质、蔬菜和适量的缓释碳水化合物为主的轻量晚餐。”他事后的专业动作是：“保持直立，散步10分钟，而不是从餐桌直接上床。”

泰特尔鲍姆医生总结了一条准则： “基本上，你的消化系统应该在你睡觉时也睡觉。”不，你不需要完美。有时早餐也很重要。

“你的生物学反应于模式而非完美——因此每周四到五次正确的晚餐时间仍然很重要。”布雷斯医生说。所以，去预订5:30的餐桌吧。你并非变成了祖父母，只是终于听从了自己的生物钟。
articles.summary:
What time do you eat dinner? Early or late? Between work and kids and everything else going on in your life, it might just be whenever you can squeeze it into your schedule, no matter what time it is. Well, you might want to rethink that.

A recent YouGov poll found that 71% of respondents typically eat dinner at 6 p.m. or later. And for years, a 5 p.m. dinner has been shorthand for early-bird specials, senior discounts and a restaurant so empty you basically had the place to yourself. It was the meal you teased your parents and grandparents about, not something you engaged in yourself.

But scroll TikTok right now and you’ll find young professionals proudly logging off work and sitting down to eat while the sun’s still up, posting it under #EarlyDinner. Recent OpenTable data backs up what your feed is telling you: 53% of Gen Zers and 51% of Millennials say they’re especially interested in earlier reservations, and in New York City, 5 p.m. bookings have jumped 20%. A Chase Travel report went so far as to declare that “5:30 p.m. is the new 8 p.m.”

So who’s right? Is it the retirement community sitting down to an early post-golf-game supper (and Gen Zers filming their 5 p.m. reservations), or the majority of Americans sticking to the OG version of dinnertime? We asked experts to settle this debate once and for all. Ahead, five medical professionals, including experts in sleep health, neuroscience and psychology, give us the the lowdown on the right time to eat dinner—and why it’s so important.

Read on to find out exactly when you should sit down to dine.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more lifestyle debates, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

Does it really matter what time you eat dinner?

Yes. The experts we spoke with kept coming back to one idea: Your body runs on a roughly 24-hour internal clock—your circadian rhythm—and it governs far more than when you feel alert or sleepy. It also shapes how you handle food.

“Melatonin secretion, which signals the body to prepare for sleep, is suppressed by both light and food intake,” explains Sarah Boss, MD, a psychiatrist and the clinical director at The Balance rehab clinic. In other words, getting the timing right between dinner and bedtime really makes a difference.

So what is the best time to eat dinner?

It depends on your bedtime, but the research points overwhelmingly in one direction: earlier, and finished well before you turn in. Yep, according to science, it turns out that Gen Z (and your grandma) have stumbled onto a genuine health upgrade with those dinners before 6 p.m.

“Late eating keeps insulin elevated and delays melatonin onset,” Dr. Boss says. Eat too late and you force your body to do two jobs at once—digesting a meal and managing blood sugar, exactly when it’s trying to wind down for sleep.

It’s more personal than a single number on the clock, but it is important to get the timing right based on your life and your sleep schedule. Here’s why.

You’ll sleep better

This is the big one. “The most consistent finding is that a large meal close to sleep, within about one to two hours, is more likely to impair sleep continuity,” says Avinesh Bhar, MD, a sleep physician and the founder of Sliiip.

If you lie down with a full stomach, your digestive system is working overtime when your body wants to power down. “Digestion raises blood sugar, insulin, metabolic activity and body temperature at a time when the body should be cooling down and preparing for sleep,” says Michael Breus, PhD, a clinical psychologist and sleep specialist known as the Sleep Doctor.

There’s also a hormonal handoff happening in the background. “At night, our cortisol levels want to start dropping so that [our brain] can favor the release of melatonin instead,” says Maj. Allison Brager, PhD, a neuroscientist and the U.S. Army’s leading sleep expert. When you’re not busy digesting, she explains, those daytime processes can go offline so your sleep systems can come online.

You’ll dodge the blood-sugar roller coaster

Your body is simply worse at handling sugar after dark. Insulin sensitivity peaks in the morning and dips in the evening, so the same plate of food spikes your blood sugar higher at night than it does at midday.

The proof is dramatic: Researchers at Johns Hopkins found that a 10 p.m. dinner raised post-meal glucose by about 18% compared with a 6 p.m. dinner of the identical meal. And a follow-up study from the same team found that staying up later didn’t reverse the effect, pinning the blame on circadian misalignment rather than simply eating too close to bedtime.

In other words, when it comes to blood sugar, the actual time on the clock matters—not just how long before bed you eat. “Eating during elevated melatonin can create circadian-metabolic misalignment and is associated with poorer glucose tolerance—particularly if dinner is within two hours of habitual bedtime,” says Dr. Bhar.

You may lose weight

An early dinner is not a magic weight-loss button—your total daily intake still matters most. But timing appears to tip the scales.

In a study conducted at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, researchers found that people who ate earlier in the day lost nearly 14 pounds, compared with about 9 pounds for those eating over a longer window. And a 2026 review of 41 randomized trials and more than 2,000 participants, published in BMJ Medicine, likewise found that earlier eating beat later eating for both weight loss and fasting insulin levels.

“Given the same amount of total daily calories, eating larger meals earlier in the day will result in putting on less fat than the same amount of calories later in the day,” says Jacob Teitelbaum, MD, author of From Fatigued to Fantastic. “Eating heavier meals early in the day also suppresses your appetite hormones so you don’t overeat at night.”

Bonus? Eating early also doubles as intermittent fasting—no willpower needed. “There’s this whole push now to support intermittent fasting, eating within a 12- to 14-hour window,” says Dr. Brager. “Eating dinner early supports this without intentionally trying to.” Finish dinner in the early evening, sleep seven or eight hours, and, as she puts it, “there’s your 12-hour window of fasting right there.”

You’ll reduce acid reflux

Gravity is doing more work than you think. “When lying down, gravity no longer helps keep stomach contents below the diaphragm,” says Dr. Bhar. “Sleep also reduces swallowing and esophageal clearance, so acid or non-acid reflux is more likely to cause discomfort, leading to micro-awakenings.”

One study from Japan’s Osaka City University found that people whose dinner-to-bed gap was under three hours had nearly 7.5 times the odds of reflux disease compared with those who ate four or more hours before bedtime.

You’ll stop fighting your biology

“Our bodies were designed to have most of our calories at midday around lunch,” says Dr. Teitelbaum. “This changed as we became industrialized and moved from farms to cities. Having the main meal at lunch with a nap after was inconvenient to factory owners.”

If you eat against that ancient rhythm, you pay for it. In fact, Dr. Brager notes that “shift work is highly associated with obesity, diabetes and ulcers, and a large part of it is because of eating at times of the day when we weren’t programmed to eat.” As she bluntly puts it, “our biology has not been programmed, nor will it ever be programmed, to eat at night.”

That’s not just a shift-worker problem. Researchers at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health found that eating your last meal after 9 p.m., versus before 8 p.m., was linked to a 13% higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

Won’t eating early just make you snack later?

Possibly, but done right, an earlier dinner can actually quiet nighttime hunger, because steadier blood sugar means fewer cravings. There’s often an adjustment curve too. “Nighttime hunger after shifting to earlier dinners is usually a two-week adjustment period, during which the body’s ghrelin patterns—the hunger hormones—recalibrate,” says Dr. Boss.

Counterintuitively, it’s the late meal that can leave you hungrier. “Poor or fragmented sleep can also increase the hunger hormone ghrelin and reduce leptin, the hormone that signals fullness,” says Dr. Breus. “Eating later can sometimes make you hungrier—not less hungry—the next morning.” In one Harvard study, eating meals about four hours later increased hunger and raised the ratio of ghrelin to leptin.

If you do need a bite before bed, choose wisely. You should aim for foods that are low in sugar and high in protein, like walnuts or almonds, says Dr. Brager—not a bowl of ice cream. Dr. Breus and Dr. Bhar also like this formula: a small snack, around 150 to 200 calories, comprised of a protein and a slow carb, such as Greek yogurt with a few berries, a banana with a little nut butter or a small bowl of oatmeal. The goal, Dr. Breus says, is “to quiet genuine hunger without asking your body to digest another meal while you sleep.”

How to design your day around an earlier dinner

Shifting dinner earlier works best when the rest of your day shifts with it. A few expert-backed tweaks:

  • Front-load your calories. Make breakfast and lunch your bigger meals, and let dinner be the lightest. “Having a lighter, low-calorie meal in the evening, preferably high in proteins and complex carbohydrates and low in sugars and fats, supports deeper sleep,” says Dr. Teitelbaum.
  • Actually sit down and eat. Don’t inhale dinner standing over the sink. Giving your body time to digest is the entire point.
  • Cut off caffeine early. “You want to stop caffeine intake at least eight hours before bed,” says Dr. Brager, noting that “the half-life of caffeine is anywhere from four to six hours.”
  • Rethink the nightcap. “The best time of day to drink is in the day,” says Dr. Brager, because “alcohol most impacts your ability to enter restorative sleep.” Dr. Breus draws the line at three to four hours before bed.
  • Take a short after-dinner walk. Ten easy minutes helps blunt the blood-sugar rise after a meal.
  • Stay hydrated—but taper at night. Big fluid volumes right before bed can send you to the bathroom and fragment your sleep.
  • Ease into breakfast the next morning. An earlier, lighter dinner often means you wake up genuinely hungry—a good sign your metabolic clock is back in sync.

But what if you’re still at work at 6 p.m.?

Here’s the reassuring part: Every expert we spoke with agreed—it’s the gap that really counts, not the clock.

“Anchor the meal to your bedtime,” says Dr. Bhar. “Finishing a normal dinner about two to four hours before bed is a sensible starting range.” Dr. Brager puts the sweet spot at two to three hours before bed, adding simply, “the earlier, the better.” Dr. Boss frames it in a way that takes the pressure off entirely: “For someone going to sleep at midnight, eating at 9 p.m. is physiologically equivalent to a 6 p.m. dinner for someone sleeping at 9 p.m.”

What if your dinner genuinely can’t happen until 8 or 9 p.m. and you can’t stay up late to compensate? “Make the late dinner smaller,” says Dr. Breus. “Move more of your calories to breakfast and lunch, then choose a lighter dinner built around lean protein, vegetables and a modest portion of slower-digesting carbohydrates.” His pro move afterward: “Stay upright and take a gentle 10-minute walk afterward, rather than going directly from the dinner table to bed.”

The bottom line

Dr. Teitelbaum sums it up in a single guideline: “Basically, your digestive system should be sleeping while you are.” And no, you don’t have to be perfect. Eating early only some nights still counts.

“Your biology responds to patterns, not perfection—so four or five well-timed dinners each week still matter,” says Dr. Breus. So go ahead—book the 5:30 table. You’re not turning into your grandparents. You’re just finally listening to your body clock.
